sources.source: OpenStreetMap walking network (streets, sidewalks and paths) near major transit stops, via the Overpass API (OpenStreetMap contributors (served by the public Overpass API instances))
sources.version: The map as it stood when each tile was fetched (the Overpass answer carries its timestamp)
sources.licence: Open Database Licence (ODbL 1.0). Attribution: "© OpenStreetMap contributors". The transit_walk_tract and transit_walk_county tables are a derived database of OpenStreetMap: if they are published (in a state pack or a download), they are offered under ODbL 1.0, with the attribution, and anyone may rebuild them with visionhousing transit-walk. Maps and results made from them are produced works and carry the attribution. The raw tiles stay in the local cache and are never published.
sources.cleaning: One query per 0.1-degree tile that touches a 3/4-mile circle around a major stop: ways tagged highway, minus motorways and unbuilt, closed or private ways (list in assumptions/transit_walk.yaml), with their nodes. Ways are cut into straight segments between their nodes; repeated segments are kept once.
sources.limits: Volunteer-mapped: sidewalks and footpaths are complete in some places and missing in others, so a street without a mapped sidewalk still counts as walkable. Barriers not tagged on the map (fences, unsafe crossings) are not seen. Stops whose network is missing or fragmentary use straight-line circles, flagged as fallback.
sources.publisher: OpenStreetMap contributors (served by the public Overpass API instances)

sources.source: LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES 8), workplace area characteristics, all jobs (U.S. Census Bureau, Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government work)
sources.cleaning: Block rows are summed to 2020 tracts: total jobs, three monthly-earnings bands and 20 industry sectors. Only the tract sums are kept; the block file is deleted.
sources.limits: Counts jobs covered by unemployment insurance plus federal civilian jobs, by where people work. Self-employed people, the military and informal work are not counted. A person with two jobs counts twice. The Census Bureau adds noise to block counts for privacy; tract and county sums are much steadier.
sources.publisher: U.S. Census Bureau, Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program

sources.source: LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES 8), home-to-work flows, all jobs (U.S. Census Bureau, Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government work)
sources.cleaning: Streamed line by line; jobs (S000) are summed to pairs of counties (work county, home county or "out_of_state"). Only the county pairs are kept.
sources.limits: Links each job's workplace block to the worker's home block. The "main" file covers jobs with both ends in the state; the "aux" file adds workers who live in another state. Residents who work in another state are in that state's files, which are not read, so out-commuting across the state line is not counted. Same job coverage as the workplace file.
sources.publisher: U.S. Census Bureau, Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program

sources.source: County Business Patterns, county file (U.S. Census Bureau)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government work)

sources.limits: Counts private establishments with paid employees and their mid-March employment and yearly payroll. Government, self-employed and most farm work are left out. Small cells carry noise; the noise flag is kept. Establishments that cannot be placed in a county are left out, so counties do not add up to the state total.
sources.publisher: U.S. Census Bureau

sources.cleaning: Thousands commas and percent signs removed; "-" (no station area) left empty.
sources.limits: The requirement each town must meet (minimum unit capacity, land area, station-area share), not what it zoned. Capacity is a zoning capacity, not a forecast of homes.

sources.source: 3A Development Tracker (CSV of developments HLC links to 3A zoning) (Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (HLC))
sources.licence: Public record posted for download by the Commonwealth; mass.gov terms of use apply
sources.cleaning: Summed per town (projects, total units, net units, deed-restricted units). Developer names and addresses are not kept.
sources.limits: Compiled by HLC from third-party information and its own judgement; may not be complete. Listed projects may not reach a building permit. Mixes proposed, permitted and built projects without a stage field.
sources.publisher: Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (HLC)

sources.source: Massachusetts ADU survey composite, municipal file (CSV) (Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (HLC))
sources.version: Composite of the July 2025, January 2026 and July 2026 surveys (last modified 2026-08-12)
sources.licence: Public record posted for download by the Commonwealth; mass.gov terms of use apply
sources.cleaning: Reshaped to one row per town and survey period; "No response" gives no row (unknown is not zero). The published totals are checked against the sum of the periods.
sources.limits: Self-reported by building officials; towns answered different waves, so the 2025 period is the full year for some towns and the first half for others (cohort column). Approvals are building permits issued, not homes finished and not Building Permits Survey authorizations (attached and interior ADUs are usually alterations). Detached and attached only; interior ADUs are counted as attached. www.mass.gov refuses scripted requests (HTTP 403 on 2026-11-24); the build respects that and adds the table only from a copy saved by hand as data/raw/local/ma/ma_adu_survey.csv.
sources.publisher: Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (HLC)

sources.source: Massachusetts General Laws chapter 40A (Zoning), sections 1A, 3 and 3A (The General Court of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts)
sources.licence: Public legislative record
sources.cleaning: Read by hand. Only citations and summaries in our own words are kept, in assumptions/law/states/ma.yaml and assumptions/calibration/already_legal_ma.yaml.
sources.limits: The statute says what zoning may not do; it does not say how each town's bylaw reads today or how often permits are refused. Boston is not subject to chapter 40A. The web text is unofficial.

sources.source: Acts of 2024, chapter 150 (the Affordable Homes Act), session law text (The General Court of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts)
sources.licence: Public legislative record
sources.cleaning: Read by hand: sections 7 and 8 (ADU definition and by-right ADU paragraph) and section 143 (effective 180 days after the act, so 2025-02-02). Kept as citations and our own summaries in assumptions/law/states/ma.yaml.
sources.limits: Gives the amending sections and their effective dates, not how towns implemented them.
sources.publisher: The General Court of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts

sources.source: Building Permits Survey, place (permit office) annual files by census region (U.S. Census Bureau)
sources.version: 2012-2025 annual files (the 2025 file is the latest published)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government work)
sources.cleaning: Two header rows joined; columns read by name. Offices keyed by state code and six-digit office id, matched to census places by state and place code. Only the offices used and their yearly aggregates are kept in outputs; raw files stay in data/raw/bps_place/.
sources.limits: Counts units authorized by each permit office, not units built. An office is a city, town, township or a county's unincorporated area; offices that did not report some months are partly imputed. One file per region and year (Northeast, Midwest, South, West; region_dir is the folder name with %20 for the space).
sources.publisher: U.S. Census Bureau

sources.source: Montgomery County (PA) sewer service areas, July 2022 edition (via PASDA) (Montgomery County, Pennsylvania (Planning Commission); served by PASDA)
sources.licence: Public county record distributed through PASDA, Pennsylvania's official open geospatial clearinghouse; the service metadata states no use constraint. Credited to Montgomery County. Only per-tract shares of homes are kept.
sources.cleaning: All 42 polygons, thinned by the server to about 5 m. 2020 Census blocks are placed by their internal point; shares are of 2020 housing units.
sources.limits: A planning map of areas served by public sewer as of 2022; it does not show spare treatment or conveyance capacity, and a parcel inside an area may still need an extension. Homes outside every polygon are read as outside public sewer (the county inventory is treated as complete).
sources.publisher: Montgomery County, Pennsylvania (Planning Commission); served by PASDA

sources.source: Adams County (PA) sewer service areas (existing), county GIS (Adams County, Pennsylvania (Office of Planning and Development GIS))
sources.licence: Public county record; the county's notice says the data are for information only and that any service area should be verified with the provider. No redistribution limit is stated. Only per-tract shares of homes are kept.
sources.cleaning: Type = 'Existing' polygons only, thinned to about 5 m.
sources.limits: Approximate locations of public or community sewer from several authorities. The 17 "Future Sewer Service Area" polygons are left out; only the 36 existing areas count.
sources.publisher: Adams County, Pennsylvania (Office of Planning and Development GIS)

sources.source: Philadelphia Water Department statement of citywide sewer service (Philadelphia Water Department)
sources.licence: Public statement of a city agency; quoted briefly, nothing else is kept
sources.cleaning: Every Philadelphia block with homes is read as inside public sewer service.
sources.limits: A whole-city statement of the utility's service territory ("supplies drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater services to customers within the City of Philadelphia"; its wastewater page adds "combined sewers in approximately half of the city's neighborhoods and a separate sewer system in the other half"), not a parcel map: a few properties on private on-lot systems would not show. It says nothing about capacity for added homes or about combined-sewer overflow limits.
sources.publisher: Philadelphia Water Department

sources.source: City of Philadelphia permit fee schedules (L&I construction and zoning fee summaries, building permit fee page, Development Impact Tax page) (City of Philadelphia (Department of Licenses and Inspections; Department of Revenue))
sources.version: PG_012_INF Rev 7.2026 (effective 2026-10-01); PZ_008_INF Rev 7.2026 (effective 2025-01-01); pages as read 2026-11-26
sources.licence: Public fee schedules of the City of Philadelphia; amounts cited with short quotes, documents not copied
sources.cleaning: Amounts copied by hand into assumptions/fee_schedules.yaml with a quote each; the check re-fetches the documents and confirms every quote and PDF checksum.
sources.limits: Summaries of fees for common projects, not the Administrative Code itself. Fees that depend on the applicant's own cost estimate (electrical work) are priced from ledger costs. Streets Department street-opening permits are not reviewed.
sources.publisher: City of Philadelphia (Department of Licenses and Inspections; Department of Revenue)

sources.source: Philadelphia Water Department Rates and Charges (effective 2026-09-01) and Regulations Chapter 5 (sewer connection fees) (City of Philadelphia, Water Department)
sources.version: Rates and Charges effective 2026-09-01; Regulations Chapter 5 as read 2026-11-26
sources.licence: Public tariff and regulations of the City of Philadelphia; amounts cited with short quotes
sources.cleaning: Amounts copied by hand into assumptions/fee_schedules.yaml with a quote each.
sources.limits: Connection, meter and plan review charges only; the size of each prototype's water service and meter is a team design assumption with a low and a high reading.
sources.publisher: City of Philadelphia, Water Department

sources.source: Pittsburgh Water and Sewer Authority, Permits page (residential permit fee, typical tap and meter cost) (Pittsburgh Water and Sewer Authority)
sources.licence: Public web page of a municipal authority; two amounts cited with short quotes
sources.cleaning: Amounts copied by hand into assumptions/fee_schedules.yaml with a quote each.
sources.limits: Only the single-family residential permit fee and the typical single-family tap and meter cost. The authority's 2026 permitting fee schedule is a PDF, and robots.txt disallows every PDF, so larger services stay unknown.
sources.publisher: Pittsburgh Water and Sewer Authority

sources.source: Vermont known wastewater service areas in towns with zoning and subdivision rules (HOME Act map, 2023) (Vermont Agency of Commerce and Community Development (published by VCGI))
sources.version: 2023-08 (polygons dated by their own sources, 2003 to 2023)
sources.licence: Public state record published by the Vermont Center for Geographic Information; no licence is stated on the item. Credited to Vermont ACCD. Only per-tract shares of homes are kept.
sources.cleaning: All 104 polygons, thinned to about 5 m.
sources.limits: Covers only towns with both zoning and subdivision rules, and each polygon is as old as its source (many 2008). Homes outside every polygon stay unknown rather than outside. No capacity information.
sources.publisher: Vermont Agency of Commerce and Community Development (published by VCGI)

sources.source: Vermont existing wastewater service areas, statewide compilation (ACCD open data, 1993-2008) (Vermont Agency of Commerce and Community Development, Department of Housing and Community Development (layer credit: Regional Planning Commissions and DHCD; published on the ANR map server))
sources.version: 1993-2008 (polygon dates in sGISDATE; 27 undated; Chittenden County 1996)
sources.licence: Public state record; no licence or use constraint is stated on the layer, so only derived aggregates (shares of homes per tract or town) may be kept or published, never the polygons themselves.
sources.cleaning: Not fetched by a build yet; attributes read once (system name, owner, source, date).
sources.limits: Old and mixed: 138 polygons compiled by the regional planning commissions, dated 1993 to 2008, with different meanings (area connected, an ordinance's 200-foot buffer, a district from a town plan). Says nothing about water service or spare capacity; not current connection status. Read so far by attributes only (2026-11-26); not used in any pack or estimate (the pack's sewer shares come from vt_accd_wastewater_service_areas).
sources.publisher: Vermont Agency of Commerce and Community Development, Department of Housing and Community Development (layer credit: Regional Planning Commissions and DHCD; published on the ANR map server)

sources.source: Pennsylvania public water supplier service areas (DEP, via PASDA) (Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection; served by PASDA)
sources.licence: Public state record (credited to PA DEP) distributed through PASDA; no use constraint is stated. Only per-tract shares and provider names are kept.
sources.cleaning: All 1,792 polygons, thinned to about 5 m; PWS ids prefixed with PA for links.
sources.limits: Present service-area boundaries of public water systems, made for the State Water Plan to find self-supplied areas; not a statement of spare supply. A home inside an area may still need a main extension.
sources.publisher: Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection; served by PASDA

sources.source: Pennsylvania DEP Act 537 official plan status (plan age by municipality) (Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection)
sources.licence: Public state record (PDF tables on DEP's website); no reuse limit stated
sources.cleaning: Six regional PDF tables read with pypdf; rows matched to municipalities by name within the county (2,534 of 2,569 matched on 2026-11-24).
sources.limits: Gives only the date DEP last approved each municipality's official sewage facilities plan (or a pre-1971 county plan) and DEP's age class. An old plan is not a ban, and a recent plan is not spare capacity.
sources.publisher: Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection

sources.source: EPA sewersheds of the United States (version 1.3) and their endpoint treatment plants (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Research and Development, Office of Water))
sources.licence: U.S. government work; the data and code are also released under the MIT licence
sources.cleaning: The state's sewersheds (STATE_CODE) thinned to about 5 m; endpoint plants with their authority and NPDES permit, giving the plant's EPA ECHO page as an official listing.
sources.limits: Context only. Most boundaries are modelled with machine learning from hexagons of about 0.11 square km (Pennsylvania: 799 of 838 modelled; Vermont: 92 of 93 taken from a 2009 state map); EPA says they are not an authoritative source for property-level connections. Never used for a tract's sewer status.
sources.publisher: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Research and Development, Office of Water)

sources.source: EPA Clean Watersheds Needs Survey 2022, documented needs by county (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Water))
sources.version: 2022 survey (needs as of January 1, 2022, in January 2022 dollars)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government work)
sources.cleaning: Categories added up: treatment (I, II), sewer repair (III-A, III-B), new collector and interceptor sewers (IV-A, IV-B), combined sewer overflow (V), stormwater, decentralized, nonpoint source, total.
sources.limits: Capital needs states documented for the survey (projects eligible for Clean Water State Revolving Fund loans), summarized by county by EPA. Context only: a large need is not a shortage of capacity, and a zero can mean nothing was submitted.
sources.publisher: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Water)

sources.source: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (flood hazard zones and NFHL availability), public map service (Federal Emergency Management Agency)
sources.version: The layer as read (FEMA updates it continuously; the read date is kept per county)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government work); FEMA's map service is keyless
sources.cleaning: Polygons with SFHA_TF = 'T' touching each county's box, in Albers (EPSG:5070), thinned by the server to 5 m, burned onto a 30 m grid by cell centre; nothing is stored but counts and answer checksums.
sources.limits: The Special Flood Hazard Area is the regulatory 1% annual chance floodplain; it leaves out flooding from heavy rain away from mapped streams, and some maps are decades old. Where FEMA has no digital map (outside layer 0, "NFHL availability") flood shares are left blank rather than zero.
sources.publisher: Federal Emergency Management Agency

sources.source: USGS Annual NLCD land cover and fractional impervious surface (Collection 1), MRLC coverage service (U.S. Geological Survey (Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium))
sources.version: Annual NLCD year 2025 (the latest year in the service's time list on 2026-11-24)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government work)
sources.cleaning: One uncompressed GeoTIFF per county box on the NLCD's own grid; land is every cell but open water and no data; shares are cell counts per tract.
sources.limits: Satellite classification at 30 m: small lots, narrow streets and tree-covered yards are blurred; the developed classes include parks and lawns (class 21). Screening only.
sources.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey (Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium)

sources.source: USGS 3D Elevation Program bare-earth elevation (3DEPElevation image service) (U.S. Geological Survey (The National Map))
sources.version: 3DEP DEMs published as of the read date (the service said October 26, 2026)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government work)
sources.cleaning: One float32 GeoTIFF per county box on the 30 m Albers grid; slope by central differences; cells next to missing elevation are left out.
sources.limits: Resampled by the service to 30 m (bilinear), so short steep banks are smoothed and the steep share is a lower bound for small sites. Screening only.
sources.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey (The National Map)

sources.source: Wyoming Statutes Titles 15 and 18 (city, town and county zoning) and session bill digests (Wyoming State Legislature)
sources.version: Text read 2026-11-24 (statutes as compiled after the 2026 budget session)
sources.licence: Public legislative record
sources.cleaning: Read by hand: W.S. 15-1-601 to 15-1-611, 18-5-201 to 18-5-208 and 18-5-303, and the 2025 and 2026 subject indexes and bill digests. Only citations and summaries in our own words are kept, in assumptions/law/states/wy.yaml.
sources.limits: The statutes say what cities, towns and counties may regulate, not what each local code allows today. Wyoming has no state ADU, missing-middle, transit-density, parking or fee statute, so this source supports a finding of silence, not a share of lots. The web PDFs are unofficial compilations.
sources.publisher: Wyoming State Legislature

sources.source: Vermont Acts 152 (S.325) and 179 (S.328) of 2026, as enacted, with their bill status pages (Vermont General Assembly)
sources.version: As enacted (Act 152 signed June 16, 2026; Act 179 signed June 18, 2026; both effective July 1, 2026). Text and bill status pages re-read 2026-11-25
sources.licence: Public legislative record
sources.cleaning: Read by hand: Act 152 Sec. 6 (10 V.S.A. § 6081(dd), the Act 250 interim housing exemption extended to January 1, 2028) and Sec. 23 (effective dates); Act 179 Sec. 9 (24 V.S.A. § 4412(1)(E), owner-occupancy words struck from the ADU rule), Sec. 9a and Sec. 14 (effective dates). Kept as dated records with citations and our own summaries in assumptions/law/timeline.yaml.
sources.limits: The acts say what changed in law and from when; they do not say how many towns have updated their bylaws or how many projects used the Act 250 exemption. The enacted PDFs mark changes by strike-through and underline; the meaning of a struck word is read from those marks by hand. The web copies are not the official printed session laws.
sources.publisher: Vermont General Assembly

sources.source: Philadelphia Zoning Base Districts, current layer (map service) (City of Philadelphia, Department of Planning and Development)
sources.version: Current when read (layer edited 2026-11-26); the edit and read dates are stored with the cached file
sources.licence: City of Philadelphia License ("Public Use; Free"; the City reserves all rights in the database and gives no title to it; data as is, without warranty). Retrieval and analysis: allowed. Redistribution of the raw outlines: not granted, so they stay in the local cache. Derived counts and shares: published with attribution, to be confirmed with the City before release
sources.cleaning: Read by object id in chunks of 100 (code, long_code, zoninggroup, pending, pendingbill), outlines generalised by the service to about 0.5 m in longitude and latitude (NAD83). Only block-by-district counts derived from it enter the pack.
sources.limits: A map of district codes, not of what each district allows; the Zoning Code (Title 14) says that, and it is published only on a commercial code host, which is not read. The City notes the boundaries are self-reported. Pending remapping bills are flagged by the layer (pending, pendingbill) and not applied.

sources.source: Philadelphia Zoning Base Districts, dated snapshots (December 2021 used) (City of Philadelphia, Department of Planning and Development)
sources.version: Snapshot zoning_basedistricts_122021 (the City's December 2021 copy; layer edited 2024-06-26)
sources.licence: City of Philadelphia License, as for the current layer: raw outlines kept locally; derived counts only in the pack
sources.cleaning: Same as the current layer.
sources.limits: A snapshot of the map on the date in its name; when a district changed between snapshots is not recorded in it. The City publishes snapshots from March 2015 to December 2025; one is read.
sources.publisher: City of Philadelphia, Department of Planning and Development

sources.source: Philadelphia Zoning Overlays (map service) (City of Philadelphia, Department of Planning and Development)
sources.licence: City of Philadelphia License, as for the base districts: raw outlines kept locally; derived counts only in the pack

sources.licence: City of Pittsburgh licence notice: for informational purposes, no guarantee of completeness or accuracy, the user indemnifies the City; nothing on redistribution. Retrieval and analysis: allowed. Raw outlines: kept in the local cache. Derived counts and shares: published with attribution

What each district allows is in the Pittsburgh Code, Title Nine, published only on a commercial code host, which is not read; Ordinance 31 of 2026 (registry pgh_legistar) is read. One polygon is the Borough of Mount Oliver, an enclave with its own zoning (treated as unmatched).

sources.licence: City of Pittsburgh licence notice, as for the zoning districts
sources.cleaning: Read like the zoning districts (name, reduction).
sources.limits: Nine areas where the old Chapter 914 parking minimums were reduced (25%, 50% or 100%, some for all uses except residential). Since Ordinance 31 took effect (October 29, 2026) there is no automobile parking minimum to reduce.

sources.source: TIGER/Line 2020 tabulation block outlines (sample counties only) (U.S. Census Bureau)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government work)
